answer.text: Spreading bond purchases across staggered maturities to manage reinvestment and interest-rate risk

explanation.text: The Logic: A bond ladder is a fixed-income strategy in which an investor buys bonds with staggered maturity dates — for example, equal allocations maturing in years 1, 2, 3, 4, and 5. As each "rung" matures, the proceeds are reinvested at the long end of the ladder. The result is a steady stream of maturities (and cash flows) and an averaging-in of prevailing yields, which together moderate both reinvestment risk and interest-rate risk. The Trap: Holding a single bond concentrates both maturity and reinvestment risk on one date. Short-selling bonds is a directional speculative position, not a laddering strategy. Holding only long-duration bonds maximises interest-rate exposure rather than smoothing it. Note: The NISM-Series-XXI-A PMS Distributors workbook (Sep 2025) discusses interest-rate risk, reinvestment risk, and diversifying fixed-income holdings across maturities (around pages 22-23 and 58-59) but does not specifically define or use the "bond ladder" term. The framing above is general fixed-income portfolio-construction knowledge.
